'''Gary William Gibbons''' (born 1 July 1946)<ref name="whoswho">
{{Who's Who | author=Anon| title=Gibbons, Prof. Gary William  | id = U17017 | year = 2014 | doi =10.1093/ww/9780199540884.013.17017 | edition = online [[Oxford University Press]]|location=Oxford}}</ref> is a British [[theoretical physics|theoretical physicist]].<ref name="scopus">{{Scopus|id=7201641657}}</ref><ref>''Euclidean Quantum Gravity'', [http://www.worldscibooks.com/physics/1301.html World Scientific (Singapore, 1993)] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120519211330/http://www.worldscibooks.com/physics/1301.html |date=19 May 2012 }}; Paperback {{ISBN|981-02-0516-3}}</ref>

==Education==
Gibbons was born in [[Coulsdon]], Surrey. He was educated at [[Purley High School for Boys|Purley County Grammar School]]<ref name="whoswho"/> and the [[University of Cambridge]], where in 1969 he became a research student under the supervision of [[Dennis William Sciama|Dennis Sciama]]. When Sciama moved to the [[University of Oxford]], he became a student of [[Stephen Hawking]], obtaining his PhD from Cambridge in 1973.<ref name="gibbonsphd"/>

==Career and research==
Apart from a stay at the [[Max Planck Institute for Physics|Max Planck Institute]] in Munich in the 1970s he has remained in Cambridge throughout his career, becoming a full professor in 1997, a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] in 1999,<ref name="royal"/> and a Fellow of [[Trinity College, Cambridge]] in 2002.

Having worked on classical general relativity for his PhD thesis, Gibbons focused on the quantum theory of black holes afterwards. Together with [[Malcolm Perry (physicist)|Malcolm Perry]], he used thermal [[Green's function]]s to prove the universality of thermodynamic properties of horizons, including cosmological event horizons.<ref>
{{cite journal
| title = Cosmological Event Horizons, Thermodynamics, and Particle Creation
| author = Gibbons, G. W., [[Stephen Hawking|Hawking, S. W.]]
| journal = [[Physical Review D]]
| volume = 15 | issue = 10 | pages = 2738–2751
|year = 1977
| doi = 10.1103/PhysRevD.15.2738
|bibcode = 1977PhRvD..15.2738G | doi-access = free
}}</ref> He developed the [[Euclidean quantum gravity|Euclidean approach]] to quantum gravity with [[Stephen Hawking]], which allows a derivation of the [[Black hole thermodynamics|thermodynamics of black holes]] from a [[functional integral]] approach.<ref>
{{cite journal
| title = Action Integrals and Partition Functions in Quantum Gravity
| author = Gibbons, G. W., [[Stephen Hawking|Hawking, S. W.]]
| journal = [[Physical Review D]]
| volume = 15 | issue = 10 | pages = 2752–2756
|year = 1977
| doi = 10.1103/PhysRevD.15.2752
|bibcode = 1977PhRvD..15.2752G }}</ref> As the [[Euclid]]ean action for gravity is not positive definite, the integral only converges when a particular contour is used for [[conformal map|conformal factors]].<ref>
{{cite journal
| title = Path Integrals and the Indefiniteness of the Gravitational Action
| author = Gibbons, G. W., [[Stephen Hawking|Hawking, S. W.]], [[Malcolm Perry (physicist)|Perry, M. J.]]
| journal = Nucl. Phys. B
| volume = 138 | issue = 1  | pages = 141–150
|year = 1978
| doi = 10.1016/0550-3213(78)90161-X
|bibcode = 1978NuPhB.138..141G }}</ref>

His work in more recent years includes contributions to research on [[supergravity]], [[p-branes]]<ref>
{{cite journal
| title = Born–Infeld particles and Dirichlet p-branes
| author = Gibbons, G. W.
| journal = Nucl. Phys. B
| volume = 514| issue = 3| pages = 603–639
|year = 1998
| doi = 10.1016/S0550-3213(97)00795-5
| arxiv = hep-th/9709027
|bibcode = 1998NuPhB.514..603G | s2cid = 119331128
}}</ref> and [[M-theory]], mainly motivated by [[string theory]]. Gibbons remains interested in geometrical problems of all sorts which have applications to physics.

===Awards and honours===
Gibbons was elected a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] (FRS) in 1999. His nomination reads{{centred pull quote|Distinguished for his contributions to General Relativity and the Quantum Theory of Gravity. He played a leading role in the development of the Euclidean approach to quantum gravity and showed how it could be used to understand the thermal character of black holes and inflating universes. This revealed a deep and unexpected relationship between gravitation and thermodynamics. As part of the Euclidean quantum gravity programme, he discovered many of the known gravitational instantons and classified their properties. In the more conventional Lorentzian approach to gravity, he has studied the behaviour of solitons in gauge theories and General Relativity and has shown how supersymmetry leads to Bogomolny inequalities on the masses and charges. More recently he has been investigating the role of topology in gravity and has obtained important restrictions on how the topology of spacetime can change. He is recognised world wide as a leader in the field.<ref name="royal"/>}}

In 2025, he was awarded the [[Dirac Medal (ICTP)]].<ref>[https://www.ictp.it/news/2025/8/2025-ictp-dirac-medal-goes-gravity-explorers Dirac Medal (ICTP) 2025]</ref>
